thread.t16.1.resolution: both withdrew unhurried into the reeds, no pursuit

thread.t22.1.text: The giant Old Man followed Alaric's retreat out of the wallow at a deliberate walk, held its distance down the lane, then charged from the wallow's edge.

thread.t23.1.text: A weir of cut poles and withy screens stands in the pool by the alder line: someone fishes these flats and may be nearby.

thread.t27.1.text: Something alive is knocking softly and rhythmically against the inside of the weir's trap cage, bump, bump, bump.
thread.t27.1.resolution: Alaric looked into the cage and saw the coot was the knocker

thread.t29.1.text: The weir fisherman points Alaric to the big gray boar rooting along the third weir since dawn; fresh trail winds toward the river-side pools
thread.t29.1.resolution: Alaric followed the trail to the third weir and found the gray boar there.

thread.t32.1.text: Something large breathes slowly in the dense reed stand north of the boar pool, unseen — likely the Old Man asleep or near it

thread.t53.1.text: Churned marsh-cat prints lead into the eight-foot reed bed past the last stakes and do not come out anywhere visible; the fisherman does not go in, warning the mud under the reeds is worse
thread.t53.1.resolution: the marsh cat was killed by Alaric's Arcane Bolt on the tussock island

thread.t63.1.text: The last gray reed-bed boar is half-crippled, bleeding freely, hind leg dragging, but still faces Alaric with tusks low on the causeway planks.
thread.t63.1.resolution: Alaric's Arcane Bolt caught it in the throat as it gathered for a last charge; it died mid-step against the weir timber.

thread.t68.1.text: Large fresh boar tracks leave the far end of the third weir north into the reed beds — a big reed-bed boar moving that way

inputs.input: I cast Arcane Bolt at the wounded boar.
With the count at 4/4, I leave the big thing in the reed stand alone and head back along the causeway toward the Guild hall in Valedorn Crown to turn in the boar cull contract.
I ask the clerk what contracts are on the board suitable for a Novice mage.
I accept the Marsh Cat cull contract at the Fish-Drying Stakes.
I sell Hesk the Old Man's tusk and the F-Rank Reed-bed Boar Hide, then head south past the tanning yards to the fish-drying stakes.
I accept Hesk's twelve-copper offer for the tusk and hide, then take up a position near the drying stakes and watch the reed stand for the marsh cat as dusk falls.
I cast Arcane Bolt at the marsh cat while it's turning back toward the reeds.
I move toward the reed stand to close to MEDIUM range, then cast Arcane Bolt at the marsh cat.
I gather the pelt, claws and fang from the marsh cat, thank the fisherman for his word to the Guild, and head back north to the Guild hall in Alderwatch to turn in the cull contract.
I ask the clerk what Novice contracts are on the board for tomorrow.
I accept the Pale Ghouls cull contract, then ask the clerk where I can find a cheap bed for the night.
I head to the Wheatsheaf, take a room for eight copper, and sleep until morning.

roomSteps.prose:
The widow looked up from her hearth when the coins came out. He counted eight copper onto the counter, and she swept them into her apron pocket with the same quick fingers as before.

Then she only looked at him.

"That's coin for the room, is it?" She wiped her hands on her apron. "Only — you paid me for last night already, love. Eight copper, before you went up. I'd have remembered twice." She frowned at the pocket, then at him, doing sums. "If it's tonight you're wanting, that's fine, but it's early yet — sun's barely down. And the second-door room's yours from last night's key, so there's nothing new to pay unless you mean a different bed."

The cat opened one eye in its chair. Outside, the street noise of the square had faded to cart-rattle and a dog somewhere, and the lamp by the counter hissed softly.

She waited, hand flat on the counter, the eight copper still in her apron. "So. Is it tonight you're booking, or have I had your coin twice for one bed?"

She drew the eight copper back out of her apron and set them on the counter between them, not pocketing them.

"Tonight, then." She nodded toward the stairs. "Second door's free tonight, same as last — eight copper for the bed, porridge a copper if you're down before the lads eat it all." She folded her hands on the counter over the coins and waited. "But it's your coin that does the booking, love. Say it's for tonight and leave them sitting there, and the room's yours."

The fire ticked in the grate. The cat stretched, yawned, and resettled itself with its back to them both.

roomSteps.prose:
"That's it, then." She swept the eight copper into her apron at last and took the key from its hook, then thought better of it and pushed it back toward him across the counter. "You'll have last night's key still. Second door, same room. Porridge if you're down early — and I mean early, the lads in back eat like gulls."

The stairs creaked the same as before. The candle stub on the stool was fresh, or fresh enough, and the shutter went shut with its click. The tick smelled of last night faintly, of him now, and the blanket was where he'd folded it.

Sleep came slow this time, the street outside still half-awake — a hammer somewhere, children shouting in the square — and then it didn't come at all for a while and then it came all at once.

He woke to grey light in the shutter seams and bread-smell again, and under it the sound of men's voices and spoons in bowls below. The heaviness was gone out of him entirely: the ache behind his eyes, the weariness in his arms and shoulders, all of it, so that lying still felt strange, like wearing borrowed clothes. His breath came deep and easy. When he flexed his fingers, the old strength ran down them clean to the tips.

Through the floorboards, the widow's voice: "Mind the pot, Tam, mind it—" and the clatter of the lad in back knocking something anyway.

The key sat where he'd left it. Morning waited outside the shutter.
